stances.claim: The 2019 polls were 'generally peaceful and orderly' only 'compared with prior exercises' -- that operative phrase is what reconciles the apparent contradiction with the next sentence's vote-buying, glitches, and overvoting findings.

The Supreme Court's 2002-2004 trio invalidating Comelec contracts -- Comelec v. Quijano-Padilla, Information Technology Foundation v. Comelec (CJ-authored), and Brillantes v. Comelec -- was correct despite knowing it would force reversion to manual elections, because 'Fiat justitia ruat caelum' obligated the Court to police 'inexplicable haste' and statutory violation even at administrative cost.
stances.confidence: asserted with named precedent and quoted holding

stances.claim: Melo deserves the title 'Father of Automated Elections in the Philippines' because, despite the Comelec's many SC defeats and incessant PCOS criticism, he accepted the 2008 chairmanship at personal reputational risk, courageously automated the 2010 presidential election after the ARMM trial run, and over successive cycles built the institutional foundation that today -- with VCM upgrades and improved transparency -- produces 'credible' elections.

The 2010 automation succeeded 'warts and all' because the critical political test -- opponent acceptance of the new president -- was met without protest; subsequent cycles have improved iteratively, with 2018 VCM modernization and 2019 Comelec transparency representing significant institutional progress.
stances.rhetorical_move: outcome-acceptance test (the operational definition of success)

notable_anecdotes: The opening exchange with readers -- 'Friends and readers challenged the opening sentence of my column last Sunday' -- converting reader pushback into the column's pedagogical occasion (the 'operative part' of comparative phrasing).

The Court's 'initially hesitant to promulgate its judgment because it would surely lead to the cancellation of automation and to a reversion to manual election' -- yet 'tasked me to write the decision' under the banner 'let justice be done though the heavens may fall' -- making CJ the protagonist of the very judgment that forced 2004 and 2007 to be conducted 'mano-mano.'

The 2010 ground-truth catalogue -- 'Too many PCOS machines failed to function properly; compact flash (CF) cards were missing; ballots were late, or spoiled by dirt, perspiration and careless handling; names of candidates were misprinted and ovals misaligned' -- physicalizing the operational chaos that nonetheless produced a legitimate succession.
Melo's voluntary early retirement 'to give his replacement sufficient time to plan the new polls' -- institutional-handover ethic offered as part of the founder's legacy.
Anchoring the tribute to Melo's '87th birthday on May 30' -- a public-occasion peg that converts the historical recital into birthday honor.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban replies to readers who challenged the opening sentence of his prior column -- 'Compared with prior exercises, the last elections were generally peaceful and orderly' -- by clarifying that 'Compared with prior exercises' is the operative part: today's vote-buying, automation glitches, and overvoting are real, but the appropriate comparison is to the manual-era cheating that automation replaced. He traces the legislative-judicial chronology: Congress enacted RA 8436 on December 22, 1997, mandating automation; the Comelec entered three contracts for the 2004 polls -- to clean the voters' list, automate counting and canvassing, and hasten vote transmission -- but the Supreme Court invalidated all three in Comelec v. Quijano-Padilla (Sept. 18, 2002), Information Technology Foundation v. Comelec (Jan. 13, 2004), and Brillantes v. Comelec (June 15, 2004), with the middle case (which CJ authored) being most crucial for its finding of 'inexplicable haste, without adequate checking and observing mandatory financial, technical and legal requirements... in violation of law and jurisprudence.' The Court was 'initially hesitant' because invalidation would force reversion to manual elections, but invoked 'Fiat justitia ruat caelum' to fulfill its duty -- and indeed the 2004 and 2007 polls were conducted 'mano-mano.' RA 9369 then updated RA 8436, and retired SC Justice Jose A. R. Melo was named Comelec chair in 2008. Under Melo the ARMM 2009 special polls were first automated, and the 2010 presidential election was 'courageously' automated despite PCOS failures, missing CF cards, late or spoiled ballots, misprinted candidate names, and misaligned ovals -- yet succeeded 'warts and all' because no opponent protested the new president's installation. Melo voluntarily retired early to give his successor planning time. The 2013 and 2016 elections were 'humped with difficulties' (source-code-review refusal, restricted random manual audit, parallel-count aversion); in 2018 the PCOS was modernized and renamed Vote-Counting Machines, and in 2019 the Comelec became 'more transparent, accountable and tolerant of criticisms.' Anchoring the tribute to Melo's 87th birthday on May 30, CJ declares that for 'daring the odds and succeeding,' Melo 'should be recognized as the Father of Automated Elections in the Philippines.'
